Ukraine: Washington offered NATO in exchange for the Donbas, Zelensky reveals, a first in the negotiations

On Saturday, November 14, the Ukrainian presidency published remarks by Volodymyr Zelensky: American negotiators asked him whether Ukraine would leave the Donbas in exchange for joining NATO. It is the first time the Alliance has been linked to territorial concessions, following the talks in Abu Dhabi. Kyiv still refuses to give up its territory [1][2][3].

Volodymyr Zelensky made these remarks to journalists on Friday; they were made public on Saturday. According to him, the question was raised for the first time during the talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi [1][2].
“That is why I think NATO is back on the agenda,” the Ukrainian president summed up [3].

He points out that Ukraine is opposed in principle to giving up territory. But if the United States and the other allies guarantee its security, its right to a well-funded army and funds for reconstruction, he would put the whole package to a referendum [3][4].

Zelensky does, however, reject any neutrality, which would require changing the Constitution. He is also wary of a new European security framework mentioned by Washington: “It can be dangerous. It must not be the main topic,” he said [4].
Washington has not commented. US envoy Jared Kushner only wrote that a “lasting peace requires credible security guarantees for Ukraine” [5].

On the ground, the Ukrainian general staff announced on Saturday that on November 13 it struck the Samara oil station, where Urals oil is blended, which accounts for up to half of Russian exports, as well as the Lipetsk-2 air base [6].

Key takeaway: until now, peace plans linked giving up the Donbas to renouncing NATO. If Washington is proposing the opposite, membership in exchange for territory, it is a major change of logic, even if the idea has yet to be confirmed on the American side [1][3][5].

Russia is hostile to it: it demands that Ukraine leave the part of the Donbas it still controls and rejects any further NATO enlargement [5]. Donald Trump, for his part, wants Kyiv to give up the 20 to 30% of the Donbas still under Ukrainian control, a red line for Kyiv [7].

The Abu Dhabi talks only produced an agreement in principle on the largest prisoner exchange of the war, with no ceasefire [7]. Moscow is seeking to reopen the whole question of European security, which Zelensky sees as a diversion [4].
At the same time, Kyiv is hitting Russian oil revenues: according to the Ukrainian general staff, Russia's five largest refineries have been hit since October 30 [6].

Ukraine joining NATO would commit France to defending it in the event of an attack, like any ally: it would be a profound change for your security and for France's military budget. In the shorter term, Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil weigh on global supply and therefore on fuel prices.

China: Xi Jinping will host Trump and Putin together on November 19 in Shenzhen, an unprecedented three-way summit focused on nuclear weapons

The White House and the Kremlin confirmed on November 13 and 14 that Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin will meet as a trio on Thursday, November 19 in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit hosted by China. On the agenda: nuclear arsenals and Iran, not Ukraine [1][2].
It is a first: until now, the three nuclear powers had only talked one-on-one, two at a time [1].
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov gave the date of Thursday, November 19; the APEC summit is being held in Shenzhen, in southern China, on November 18 and 19 [3][2].

Donald Trump wants to discuss reducing nuclear weapons stockpiles. The last Russian-American treaty, New START, expired in February: it had capped the two countries' strategic arsenals since 2010 [2].
A senior US official warns: “We are not expecting any agreement,” the meeting is meant to be the “beginning of a conversation.” Iran will also be discussed, but not the war in Ukraine [1][2].
Dmitry Peskov considers the meeting “extremely important,” while warning that whatever is decided there cannot be “imposed” on other countries [2].

In the background is trade: Beijing has extended until January 10, 2027 the suspension of its 2025 restrictions on rare earths [4]. Chinese analysts warn that China could reactivate them if Washington tightens its limits on chips after Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia [5][6].

Key takeaway: China will host the American and Russian presidents at the same table, on its own soil. Even without an agreement, it is a prestige win for Xi Jinping, who is positioning himself as an arbiter between the other two major nuclear powers [1][2].

The nuclear issue is the most delicate one for Beijing. After the end of New START, Trump rejected the one-year extension proposed by Moscow and is calling for a new, “improved” treaty that would include China. Beijing is reluctant to join an agreement it did not negotiate [2].

The summit also comes as the US Congress is pushing to tighten the screws on chip sales to China, after the affair that cost Jensen Huang his job [6]. Beijing has powerful leverage with rare earths, which are essential to electronics and the auto industry [5][4].
Analysts expect more symbolism than concrete results [2].

Europeans will not be at the table, even though nuclear weapons and Iran concern them directly. If the meeting eases relations between Washington and Beijing, rare earths will keep arriving in European factories (electric cars, wind turbines, phones). If it goes badly and the chip war starts up again, electronics prices and industrial supply would suffer.

news.2026-11-15-roumanie-manifestation-a: Romania: thousands of far-right supporters march without authorization in Bucharest for the jailed Călin Georgescu and demand the president's departure

On Saturday, November 14, between 7,500 and more than 10,000 people gathered in Bucharest, near Parliament, at the call of the far-right AUR party, to support Călin Georgescu, a former presidential candidate held in pretrial detention. City hall had banned the demonstration and the courts had upheld the ban [1][2][3].

The rally began around 2 p.m. in Izvor Park, at the foot of the Palace of the Parliament. Police estimated it at 7,500 people, according to Mediafax; the daily Adevărul put it at around 8,000, and the G4Media website at more than 10,000 [1][2][3].
Bucharest city hall had refused to authorize the demonstration, and on Friday the Bucharest court rejected the organizers' appeal as unfounded [3][4].

George Simion, the leader of AUR, spoke while insisting that his party was not the organizer: “This is the meeting of the Romanian people,” he declared [5]. He accuses President Nicușor Dan of having the rally banned; the presidency calls this a rumor [4].

Some of the protesters then went to the detention center where Călin Georgescu is being held. They chanted slogans calling for his release and for Nicușor Dan's resignation [1][6]. About 2,000 people were there at the peak, and 400 in the evening [3][6].
A former presidential candidate, Călin Georgescu is in pretrial detention. He is under investigation for fraud and forming an organized criminal group [4].
George Simion had asked all AUR members to come to Bucharest for two days, Saturday and Sunday [7].

According to political scientist Cristian Pîrvulescu, AUR is trying to hold on to the roughly 40% of dissatisfied voters; he describes “an electorate that renews itself from one generation to the next” [8].

Key takeaway: the Romanian far right is still able to mobilize thousands of people, even in defiance of a ban. It is turning Călin Georgescu into a martyr and is directly targeting President Nicușor Dan [1][4].

The standoff is also legal: by demonstrating despite the court's decision, AUR is testing the authority of the state, while shielding itself behind the idea of a “meeting of the people” that it supposedly did not organize [3][5].

The social context helps AUR: for weeks Romania has been going through a wave of protest over the minimum wage, set at 4,325 lei gross per month since July 2026, and over austerity, which fuels the protest vote [8][9].

For Europe, Romania is a key country: a NATO member, bordering Ukraine and on the Black Sea. A far right that defies the courts and demands the head of state's departure becomes a European issue there [1][4].

Romania is on the front line of the war in Ukraine, on the eastern flank of NATO, of which France is a member: its political stability matters for your security too. And if you have Romanian relatives or colleagues, this debate over Georgescu deeply divides families there.

Algeria: Paris turns to Brussels as French goods are reportedly blocked at the border

On Friday, November 13, the French Foreign Ministry announced that France would ask the European Commission to examine whether Algeria is complying with its association agreement with the EU. Algerian importers are reportedly being refused French goods, while French exports to Algeria already fell by about 12% in 2025, to €4.2bn [1][2][3].

French Foreign Ministry spokesman Pascal Confavreux announced that Paris was referring the matter to the European Commission, which negotiates and enforces trade agreements on behalf of the 27 [1][2].

“We are asking the Commission to immediately examine the conditions for activating them,” he said, referring to the mechanisms provided for by the association agreement between the EU and Algeria [1].

According to industry professionals quoted by Le Monde, requests to import French products, or goods that have passed through French ports, are being refused by the Algerian authorities [1]. Paris is reacting to unofficial reports of a ban on imports from France; Algiers has not announced anything officially [3].

Trade was already declining: French exports fell by about 12% in 2025, to €4.2bn, and the drop continued over the first eight months of 2026, with −12% for French sales and −11% for purchases from Algeria [1].
Reuters reported in October that Algeria had allegedly ordered a halt to exports of urea, a fertilizer, to France; deliveries have stopped, according to the same sources [1][2].
On the Algerian side, part of the press denounces a “neocolonial delusion” and asserts that “Algeria is no longer the cash cow” of France [4].

Key takeaway: the row between Paris and Algiers is becoming a European affair. By going through Brussels, France is turning an unofficial boycott, which is hard to prove, into a possible violation of a trade treaty between the EU and Algeria [1][3].

The mechanism is simple: it is the Commission, not Paris alone, that runs the EU's trade policy. France is asking it to check whether the commitments made by Algiers in the association agreement are being respected, and then to activate the tools provided for by that text [1][2]. The difficulty will be proving a blockade that has never been officially announced [3].

The case is part of an up-and-down relationship. After a thaw in early 2026, with visits by French ministers to Algiers, several diplomatic and judicial episodes have strained relations again [1]. According to Africa Intelligence, Emmanuel Macron reportedly sent a diplomatic adviser in early November to meet President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, a report that has not been confirmed [5].
The decline in trade in both directions, −12% and −11% over eight months, shows that the trade relationship was already eroding before this new escalation [1].

French companies that sell in Algeria risk losing a market that was still worth €4.2bn in 2025. The halt in Algerian urea deliveries could also make fertilizer more expensive for French farmers, and eventually push up some food prices.

Colombia: 100 days after taking office, Abelardo de la Espriella keeps 48% approval but faces a national strike against his VAT increase

This weekend, November 14 and 15, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, who has made security his priority, reaches 100 days in power. An AtlasIntel poll gives him 48.3% approval, but the main trade union is calling for a national strike on November 19 against his “economic rescue law” [1][3][5].
Having taken office on August 7, 2026, succeeding Gustavo Petro, Abelardo de la Espriella focused his first 100 days on security and on the crisis caused by the August 10 earthquake [1].
His so-called “submission to justice” law, enacted on November 4, closes the door to negotiations with illegal armed groups [1].
According to an AtlasIntel poll for Bloomberg, 48.3% of Colombians approve of their president at this stage [3].
The government saw 27 changes between August 7 and November 14: 23 departures or replacements and four appointments that fell through [4].
The “economic rescue law,” designed to reduce the deficit, plans to apply the standard 19% VAT to basic basket products currently taxed at 5% or exempt. It cuts corporate tax from 35% to 31% [6].

The CUT trade union confederation is calling for a national strike on Thursday, November 19 and is demanding that the bill be withdrawn or amended [5]. Its president Fabio Arias warns that 700,000 jobs could disappear [6].
The government insists its finances are constrained: according to its “budget of truth” for 2027, out of every 100 pesos spent, 86 go to running the state and to debt [7].

Key takeaway: Abelardo de la Espriella, a hard-right figure, remains fairly popular on security, but he is entering the riskiest phase: making people pay for fixing the public finances. His VAT increase on food is bringing people onto the streets as early as November 19 [3][5][6].

Experts interviewed by Infobae believe it is too early to draw conclusions. Political scientist Juan Nicolás Garzón points to a lack of budget clarity, while consultant Juan Falkonerth welcomes the restoration of relations with several countries [1].

The reform's mechanism is classic: the state seeks quick revenue through VAT, a tax everyone pays at the checkout, while easing corporate tax to attract investment. The unions see it as shifting the burden onto low-income households; the government replies that it inherited badly managed accounts from the Petro team [6][7].

The left is also protesting against the cost of living and a cut in the minimum wage, according to the Mexican daily La Jornada [2]. The president has no majority of his own in Congress, which makes the passage of his law uncertain [8].

Colombia is a major exporter of coffee, flowers and oil to Europe. A social or budget crisis can move these prices and the value of the peso. More broadly, it is the same puzzle as in France: reducing a high deficit without triggering social anger, here by touching VAT on food, a choice that is always explosive.

Oil: for the first time since the start of the war with Iran, the IEA reports more supply than demand, and Brent posts a second weekly decline

On Friday, November 13, the Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA) announced that the global oil market is returning to surplus this quarter, a first since the start of the war with Iran. Brent ended at $95.84 a barrel, down about 2.5% over the week [1][2][3][4].
Brent, the global oil benchmark, finished Friday at $95.84 a barrel, up just 2 cents, after rising as high as $96.67 during the day [4][5].
Over the week, it lost about 2.5%: its second straight weekly decline. US crude WTI fell 0.2% on Friday, to $88.56 [1][4][9].
According to the IEA, Middle East exports are recovering faster than global demand, despite attacks on ships [2][3].
Observed global inventories rose by 52 million barrels in October, their first increase since June, according to the agency [2][6].
The IEA expects global demand to fall by 2.7 million barrels per day in 2026, to 102.3 million, then rise again by 2 million in 2027 [6].
Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that a deal with Iran was “not necessary” to end the war: he is keeping the blockade on Iranian oil and the sanctions [1].
The risk remains high: on Thursday, the Iranian military said four tankers had been hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring its warnings [1][5].

Key takeaway: the oil market is switching sides. Since the start of the war, there was a shortage of oil, and prices soared. The IEA is now saying the opposite: this quarter, there will be more barrels than buyers. Brent remains expensive, close to $96, but the trend has been downward for two weeks [1][2][4].

This reversal is a surprise. The previous month, the agency was still forecasting a deficit in the fourth quarter, Reuters notes. It now expects a larger surplus in 2027, of about 3.8 million barrels per day [2][6].

Two things could still change everything. First, attacks on ships in the Gulf, which the IEA cites as the main risk. Second, diesel: the agency considers its shortage “the dominant concern” of the market, because refineries are not keeping up [2][3].

Prices swung on Friday with contradictory signals about talks between Washington and Tehran. Keeping the US blockade in place limits Iranian sales, but the return of Gulf barrels weighs more heavily for now [1][4][5].

Falling oil prices eventually show up at the pump, but with a delay and mostly for gasoline. Diesel, on the other hand, remains tight according to the IEA: diesel prices could fall more slowly. Less inflation from energy also means less pressure on central banks to raise their rates, and therefore on your loan.

How it works: why a “surplus” pushes oil prices down

The price of oil is set every day on futures markets, in London for Brent and in New York for WTI. Buyers there bet on the future balance between supply and demand. When the IEA, which advises the major consuming countries, announces that supply exceeds demand, it means inventories are going to swell: in October, they already gained 52 million barrels [2]. With tanks filling up, no one is fighting to buy anymore, and the price falls. Conversely, a risk in the Strait of Hormuz or a tanker being hit pushes prices back up within hours, as happened during Friday's session, before Brent fell back [1][4]. That is why oil moves so much: it reacts both to figures and to fear.

Tokyo: the Nikkei gains 6.46% in one week, its best since June, despite the crisis at Nvidia, but SoftBank loses another 5%

On Friday, November 13, the Tokyo Stock Exchange's Nikkei index ended at 61,142.35 points (+0.53%) and gained 6.46% over the week, its best since mid-June. Strong corporate earnings made investors forget the resignation of Nvidia's boss. SoftBank Group, however, fell 5.11% [1][2].
The Nikkei rose 0.53% on Friday, to 61,142.35 points, and 6.46% over the week, according to Reuters [1].
It is its best week since the one ending June 15. The broader Topix index gained 0.11%, to 3,941.57 points, and 6.3% over the week [1][2][3].
Chip equipment makers held firm: Advantest gained 2.08% and Tokyo Electron 1.69% [2].
SoftBank Group, a major AI investor, lost 5.11% on Friday, after already falling 3.04% on Thursday [2][4].
On Thursday, the Nikkei had fallen 0.7%, to 60,819.84 points, as tech stocks followed Nvidia's fall [4].
Just before this rebound, the index had entered a “bear market,” after a 21% drop from its peak [5].
SoftBank is piling up bad news: a $7bn loss for the quarter and Beijing's blocking of its $5.4bn acquisition of ABB's robotics business [7][6].

Key takeaway: the Tokyo Stock Exchange has erased part of its recent fall. After losing 21% from its peak, the Nikkei has just gained 6.46% in five days. Investors focused on the strong earnings of Japanese companies rather than the turmoil at Nvidia [1][2][5].

The contrast with Wall Street is striking. In the United States, Jensen Huang's resignation sent chip stocks plunging. In Tokyo, equipment suppliers such as Advantest and Tokyo Electron instead rose on Friday [2].

SoftBank remains the weak link. Masayoshi Son's group has bet billions on AI and on power plants for data centers in the United States. On November 10 it announced a quarterly loss of about ¥1,120bn, partly due to a $3.7bn charge on these power plants [7].

Geopolitics also weighs. Beijing banned SoftBank's acquisition of the robotics division of Swiss group ABB, on security grounds; ABB hinted that tensions between China and Japan had played a role [6].

If you have a “Japan” or “Asia” fund in your life insurance policy or your PEA, it has probably recovered well this week. But the gap between the Nikkei and SoftBank shows that an index and a single stock can move in opposite directions: diversifying remains the best protection.

How it works: bear market and rebound

On the stock market, people talk about a “bear market” when an index has lost at least 20% from its high. That is what happened to the Nikkei, which fell 21% from its peak [5]. But these periods never move in a straight line: after a sharp drop, some investors consider stocks cheap again and buy back in, which triggers sharp rebounds. This week, the Nikkei gained 6.46%, driven by strong corporate earnings [1][2]. A rebound does not mean the decline is over: the rise has to last several weeks before you can talk about a real recovery. The Nikkei is very sensitive to tech and AI stocks, such as SoftBank or Advantest, which makes it more volatile than other indices [2].
